DEBATE_DATA.PRO.constructiveParagraphs[1: To define our terms: to ratify means to formally consent to be bound by a treaty, so it becomes legally binding on that country; European members of NATO are the 30 European allies in the 32-nation alliance; and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons—the TPNW—is the 2017 United Nations treaty outlawing the possession, hosting, or assistance of nuclear weapons. Nuclear deterrence—threatening nuclear retaliation to prevent attack—is a gamble with infinite stakes that requires a 100 percent success rate forever. Ratifying the TPNW replaces Cold War brinkmanship with real security for three key reasons.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.constructiveParagraphs[2: First, humanitarian risk and near misses. Deterrence relies on pure luck, not strategic genius. Lewis, 14 from Chatham House reviewed declassified documents, testimonies, and interviews across 13 near-nuclear-use crises and concluded the world 'has, indeed, been lucky'—with individual officers, 'often in disobedience of protocol and political guidance,' saving the day in cases like the 1983 Petrov satellite false alarm—and it flags modern warnings like the 2009 underwater collision between British and French nuclear submarines, and command-and-control laxity in the US Air Force revealed in 2013. Furthermore, Kristensen, 26 at the Federation of American Scientists estimates the US still stores about 100 B61 free-fall nuclear gravity bombs at six airbases in five European NATO countries—painting a preemptive, meaning first-strike, radioactive bullseye on European nations, where the Red Cross (ICRC, 20) warns radioactive fallout 'cannot be contained within national borders' and no state could adequately respond, while Rutgers-led modeling in Nature Food (Xia, Robock, and Toon, 22) estimates a US-Russia war could kill over 5 billion people through famine. Worse, Sweeney, 20 at Defense Priorities shows these gravity bombs are effectively useless because fighter jets cannot reliably penetrate Russian air defenses, while RAND's Baltic wargames found that even modernized NATO tactical—meaning shorter-range battlefield—nukes leave Russia with escalation dominance, where NATO faces the stronger pressure to back down (Davis, 19).
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.constructiveParagraphs[3: Second, conventional superiority by denial—meaning non-nuclear forces that stop an invasion on the battlefield before it succeeds. Europe does not need nuclear weapons to defend itself against Russian aggression, because denial rests on precision strike, air power, and industrial depth. SIPRI, 26 figures show NATO outspends Russia 1.58 trillion dollars to 190 billion—an 8.3-to-1 resource advantage—with the 29 European NATO members alone spending 559 billion dollars as Europe's military spending surged 14 percent in 2025. Why does that conventional superiority stop Russia? As van Hooft, 25 at RAND Europe explains, NATO's fifth-generation stealth fighter aircraft, integrated air-and-missile defense shields, and long-range conventional precision-strike missiles could target Russian units attacking NATO territory, their reinforcements, and their logistics, while denying Russia's use of missiles—raising the costs of aggression from the early stages of a conflict without ever risking mutual nuclear suicide. Meanwhile, Harvard Law's clinic (Harvard Law Clinic, 18) confirms European allies can stay in NATO's Article 5 conventional defense as long as they give up the nuclear umbrella and opt out of nuclear strike planning, matching France's posture outside NATO's Nuclear Planning Group since 1966.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.constructiveParagraphs[4: Third, financial divestment—pulling bank loans and investments out of nuclear weapons makers—and cutting off Russian nuclear revenue. We do not need Russia to sign the TPNW for it to work. Article 1(1)(e) of the treaty legally bans assisting nuclear weapons 'in any way,' which the Nuclear Weapons Ban Monitor reads to cover financing—so European ratification puts legal pressure on Europe's banks. PAX/ICAN, 23 profile 109 financial institutions already restricting nuclear weapons producers, many citing the TPNW, and institutions holding 3.9 trillion dollars named the treaty as a reason to exclude them (PAX/ICAN, 22). Even more importantly, Danylyuk, 26 at the Royal United Services Institute reveals that European Union nations still paid about 781 million euros in 2025 for enriched uranium and nuclear fuel from Russia's state corporation Rosatom—whose nuclear weapons complex employed about 38 percent of its 250,000 workers as of 2016, per SIPRI data. Ratifying the TPNW gives European governments a powerful legal and moral argument to cut off nearly 800 million euros a year flowing to the steward of Russia's nuclear weapons complex. We proudly affirm.

DEBATE_DATA.PRO.frontlines[9].response: When our opponents claim M.A.D. cancels out war or say bombs are never used because they just 'go boom,' they concede our first contention: a weapon too suicidal to ever detonate is a bluff that did not stop Russian aggression—Russian sabotage attacks across Europe nearly tripled from 2023 to 2024 (Jones, 25 at CSIS), RAND's Baltic wargames found even modernized NATO tactical nukes leave Russia with escalation dominance (Davis, 19), and Lewis, 14 at Chatham House concludes the world 'has, indeed, been lucky' in near misses like the 1983 Petrov false alarm.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.frontlines[9].finalFocus: Extend our first contention over their M.A.D. bluff: Lewis, 14 shows the world 'has, indeed, been lucky' in near misses like the 1983 Petrov false alarm, while Davis, 19 at RAND found even modernized NATO tactical nukes leave Russia with escalation dominance.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.frontlines[10].response: Extending our humanitarian impact on C1, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC, 20) warns fallout 'cannot be contained within national borders,' recovery would take 'several decades,' and no state could adequately respond; after a strike near B61 bases like Büchel, Kleine Brogel, Volkel, or Aviano, only bottled water is known to be safe until tap supplies are tested and garden crops must not be eaten until cleared (CDC, 24)—while Xia, Robock, and Toon, 22 in Nature Food estimate a US-Russia nuclear war could starve over 5 billion people. Removing Europe's roughly 100 B61 bombs (Kristensen, 26) removes that radioactive bullseye.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.frontlines[10].citation: ICRC, 20 (Red Cross), CDC, 24, Xia, Robock & Toon, 22 (Nature Food) & Kristensen, 26 (FAS)
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.frontlines[10].finalFocu: Extend our humanitarian radiation warrant: ICRC, 20 warns nuclear fallout cannot be contained within borders, CDC, 24 says tap water is unsafe until tested, and Xia, Robock, and Toon, 22 in Nature Food estimate a US-Russia war could starve over 5 billion people.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.counterDefenses[3].respo: Our opponents' nuclear ultimatum scenario forgets two strategic realities: first, this resolution applies only to European NATO members, so the United States retains its ~1,700 deployed strategic warheads on submarines, ICBMs, and bombers outside Europe (Kristensen, 26); and second, van Hooft, 25 at RAND Europe shows that conventional long-range precision missiles and stealth airpower could target Russian units, reinforcements, and logistics early in a conflict, raising the costs of any ultimatum Moscow tries to back with force.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.counterDefenses[4].respo: Our opponents promise EU nuclear sanctions that Europe has failed to pass for four straight years: Danylyuk, 26 at RUSI shows Rosatom is still largely unsanctioned after four years of war—Hungary and Slovakia block EU action—while EU states imported about 781 million euros of Russian uranium and fuel in 2025 and Germany even approved Rosatom-licensed fuel production at Lingen. Only ratifying TPNW Article 1(1)(e) gives Europe a powerful legal and moral argument to cut off nuclear warhead suppliers.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.counterDefenses[5].respo: Attributing 77 years of NATO security to nuclear gravity bombs rather than Article 5 conventional forces fails a basic credibility test: as RAND's Baltic study (Shlapak, 16) noted, it may seem highly unlikely to Moscow that an American president would trade New York for Riga. What actually deters a Russian land grab against the 23 non-nuclear European NATO allies—and what Ukraine lacked in 1994—is the certainty that crossing a NATO border immediately engages forward-stationed allied combat forces and NATO's overwhelming air and naval superiority.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.counterDefenses[6].respo: A threat that Moscow doubts NATO would execute does not deter a war—it invites one: an empty bluff that needs Nuclear Planning Group, US-President, and host-government sign-off cannot deter Putin when the jets carrying B61s cannot reliably get through Russian air defenses (Sweeney, 20)—and RAND's wargames found even modernized NATO tactical nukes leave Russia with escalation dominance (Davis, 19). Keeping B61s only paints a target on Aviano, Büchel, and the other host bases.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.counterDefenses[11].resp: Whether Putin keeps warheads in Belarus or not, matching him with B61 gravity bombs is strategically pointless: Sweeney, 20 proves the jets carrying Europe's B61 gravity bombs cannot reliably get through Russian air defenses anyway, whereas van Hooft, 25 at RAND explains NATO's conventional precision deep-strike missiles raise Russia's costs from the very first hours of a conflict.
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.crossfireTraps[0].questi: If Mutually Assured Destruction cancels out conflict, why did Russia invade Ukraine and nearly triple sabotage bombings and arson across Europe from 12 in 2023 to 34 in 2024—and how is M.A.D. a reliable shield when Chatham House concluded the world 'has, indeed, been lucky' in near misses like the 1983 Petrov false alarm?
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.crossfireTraps[1].questi: Since you just admitted nuclear bombs cannot actually be used because they simply 'go boom' and blow everything up, why should Germany lock 8.3 billion euros into F-35A jets to carry US B61 bombs whose jets can't reliably get through Russian air defenses?
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.crossfireTraps[2].questi: When the Red Cross warns nuclear fallout cannot be contained within national borders, the CDC says tap water is unsafe until tested, and Nature Food estimates a US-Russia war could starve over 5 billion people, why keep about 100 B61 bombs that make five European countries first-strike targets?
DEBATE_DATA.PRO.crossfireTraps[2].source: ICRC, 20 (Red Cross), CDC, 24, Xia, Robock & Toon, 22 (Nature Food) & Kristensen, 26 (FAS)

DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[0].takeaway: CON: Former CIA chiefs warned in 2025 that US credibility is in doubt—Panetta said a nervous Europe believes the US would not stand behind Article 5, and Brennan called the pause in intelligence for Ukraine 'a pressure tactic and extortion'—so Europe cannot abolish Britain and France's 515 warheads. PRO: If Washington won't stand behind Article 5, the roughly 100 US B61 bombs in Europe, which need US presidential release authorization (Sweeney, 20), protect little and make host bases targets, while European NATO alone outspends Russia nearly 3-to-1 overall ($559B vs. $190B).
DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[0].verbatim: Panetta (One Decision, March 6, 2025): “the message that went out both to our allies and to our adversaries is that The United States credibility is not to be relied on. I think what you're seeing is a very nervous Europe believes that The United States would not stand behind Article Five, and that's why Europe is trying to pull together in order to try to build up their own defenses…” Brennan (Times Radio, via HuffPost UK, March 6, 2025), on the pause in US intelligence sharing with Ukraine: “I see it more as a pressure tactic and extortion.” Beam (Agenda Pública, Dec 27, 2025) said the new US strategy marks a “shift from a partnership, to more of a variable, to a liability” for US partnerships in Europe. Summary (not a quote): none of them is confirmed saying, in those words, that Trump does not have NATO's back.
DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[1].citation: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), report summarizing a March 2, 2020 expert meeting, August 29, 2020.
DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[1].takeaway: PRO: Fallout from a nuclear detonation cannot be contained within national borders, recovery in or near a populated area would take several decades, and no state or international body could adequately respond; the only way to guarantee nuclear weapons are never used again is to prohibit and eliminate them.
DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[1].verbatim: “The effects of a nuclear weapon detonation, notably the radioactive fallout carried downwind, cannot be contained within national borders. The scale of destruction and contamination after a nuclear detonation in or near a populated area could cause profound social and political disruption as it would take several decades to reconstruct infrastructure and regenerate economic activities, trade, communications, health-care facilities and schools. No state or international body could address, in an appropriate manner, the immediate humanitarian emergency nor the long-term consequences of a nuclear weapon detonation in a populated area… Notably, owing to the long-lasting effects of exposure to ionizing radiation, the use or testing of nuclear weapons has, in several parts of the world, left a legacy of serious health and environmental consequences that disproportionally affect women and children… The only way to guarantee that nuclear weapons are never used again is by prohibiting and eliminating them.”
DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[2].citation: Lili Xia, Alan Robock, Kim Scherrer, Cheryl S. Harrison, Benjamin Leon Bodirsky, Isabelle Weindl, Jonas Jägermeyr, Charles G. Bardeen, Owen B. Toon and Ryan Heneghan (Rutgers-led team; Toon is at the University of Colorado), Nature Food, Vol. 3, Issue 8, pp. 586–596, August 15, 2022.
DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[2].takeaway: PRO: Soot from nuclear-war fires would disrupt the climate and cut crop, livestock and fishery output in almost all countries—so more than 2 billion people could die from an India-Pakistan war and more than 5 billion from a US-Russia war.
DEBATE_DATA.SOURCE_CARDS[2].verbatim: “Atmospheric soot loadings from nuclear weapon detonation would cause disruptions to the Earth’s climate, limiting terrestrial and aquatic food production… In quantifying impacts away from target areas, we demonstrate that soot injections larger than 5 Tg would lead to mass food shortages, and livestock and aquatic food production would be unable to compensate for reduced crop output, in almost all countries… We estimate more than 2 billion people could die from nuclear war between India and Pakistan, and more than 5 billion could die from a war between the United States and Russia—underlining the importance of global cooperation in preventing nuclear war.”
